title: CSC3710 2026-08-27 — Sets, Relations, Graphs and Recursive Definitions

questions.q: Which of the following equalities are true?
questions.explain: A set is determined only by which objects are members: listing an element twice or in another order changes nothing, and 2, 3, 5 are already natural numbers. Ordered pairs are different: (1, 2) ≠ (2, 1) because position matters.

questions.q: Which kind of object distinguishes [1, 1, 2] from [1, 2] but treats [1, 2] and [2, 1] as the same?
questions.explain: A **multiset** counts occurrences (so 1 twice ≠ 1 once) but ignores order. A set ignores both; an ordered pair cares about both.

questions.topic: Power set of the empty set
questions.q: What is 𝒫(∅)?
questions.explain: The only subset of ∅ is ∅ itself, so 𝒫(∅) = {∅}: a set with **one** element (a box containing an empty box), not the empty set.

questions.q: For every set A, the power set 𝒫(A) contains at least one element.
questions.explain: ∅ ⊆ A for every A, so ∅ ∈ 𝒫(A). Hence the smallest possible power set is {∅}, which has one element.

questions.q: Let A = {p, q, r}. How many elements does 𝒫(A) have?
questions.explain: Each of the 3 elements is independently in or out of a subset: 2 · 2 · 2 = 2³ = 8. They are ∅, {p}, {q}, {r}, {p,q}, {p,r}, {q,r}, {p,q,r}.

questions.q: What is |{a, {a}, a}|?
questions.explain: Remove the repeat: the set is {a, {a}}. The object a and the set {a} are different elements, so there are 2 distinct elements.
Cardinality counts **distinct** elements. {a, a, b} = {a, b}, so its cardinality is 2.

questions.q: For an arbitrary set A (inside some universe U), what is |A ∩ Ā|?
questions.explain: Ā = U − A contains exactly the elements of U not in A, so A and Ā share nothing: A ∩ Ā = ∅, cardinality 0. Even for A = ∅, Ā = U and ∅ ∩ U = ∅.

questions.q: Why must a complement Ā always be taken relative to a universe U?
choices: Because complements are only defined for finite sets
Because "everything not in A" only makes sense once we fix the set of all objects under discussion
Because A ∩ Ā would otherwise be nonempty
questions.explain: "Everything not in A" is meaningless until you fix what "everything" is. Defining Ā = {x ∈ U : x ∉ A} makes the complement a definite set; changing U changes Ā.

questions.q: Let U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and A = {2, 4}. What is Ā?
questions.explain: Ā = U − A: remove 2 and 4 from U, leaving {1, 3, 5}. Then A ∩ Ā = ∅ and A ∪ Ā = U.

questions.topic: Set given by a condition over ℤ
questions.q: What is |{x ∈ ℤ : x² + 5 = 0}|?
questions.explain: The equation says x² = −5, but the square of any integer (indeed any real) is ≥ 0. No element satisfies it, so the set is ∅ with cardinality 0.

questions.q: What is |{x ∈ ℝ : x² − 5 = 0}|?
questions.explain: Over the reals, x = ±√5, so the set is {−√5, √5}. Over ℤ the same equation gives ∅, since √5 is not an integer: the set after "∈" acts as the universe and changes the answer.

questions.q: What is |{x ∈ ℕ : x² = 9}|?
questions.explain: Over ℤ the solutions are −3 and 3, but −3 ∉ ℕ, so only {3} remains: cardinality 1.

questions.q: The condition in set-builder notation (e.g. x² + 5 = 0) alone determines which set is described.
questions.explain: The condition **together with its universe** determines the set. x² + 5 = 0 gives ∅ over ℤ or ℝ, but two solutions ±i√5 over ℂ.

questions.q: For nonempty sets A = {0, 1, 2} and B = {x, y}, A × B = B × A.
questions.explain: The set of pairs is unordered, but each **pair** is ordered: (0, x) ∈ A × B while B × A contains (x, 0), and (0, x) ≠ (x, 0). So A × B ≠ B × A in general.

questions.q: Let B = {x, y} and C = ∅. What is B × C?
questions.explain: A pair needs a second component from C, and C has none, so no pair can be formed: B × ∅ = ∅ (and |B × C| = 2 · 0 = 0).

questions.q: Let A = {1, 2} and B = {a, b, c}. What is |A × A × B|?
questions.explain: |A₁ × … × Aₙ| = |A₁| · … · |Aₙ|, so 2 · 2 · 3 = 12 ordered triples.

questions.q: Let A = {0, 1, 2} and B = {x, y}. Which are elements of B × A?
questions.explain: B × A has first component from B and second from A: pairs like (x, 0) and (y, 2). (0, x) is in A × B instead, and (x, y) has its second component from B, not A.

questions.q: In the formula |A × B| = |A| · |B|, what does "·" mean, and what will "·" mean for the rest of the course?
choices: Multiplication of numbers here; concatenation of strings from now on
questions.explain: Here the dot multiplies two **numbers** (cardinalities). From now on in this course "·" is applied to strings and means **concatenation**. Read the dot by what it is applied to.

questions.q: What is a binary relation on a set S?
choices: A subset of S × S that is reflexive
A function from S to S
questions.explain: **Any** subset of S × S is a binary relation on S; no further condition is needed. (A ternary relation is a subset of S × S × S.)

questions.q: Let S be a set. Which of the following are relations on S?
questions.explain: ∅ ⊆ S × S (the empty relation: nothing related) and S × S ⊆ S × S (the largest relation: everything related, including itself). {(s, s)} is a subset too. S itself is a set of elements, not of pairs, so it is not a subset of S × S.

questions.q: S = {Anne, Ben, Chris, Don}. In the directed graph of the largest relation R = S × S ("everyone knows everyone's number, including their own"), how many arrows are there?
questions.explain: |S × S| = 4 · 4 = 16 ordered pairs, one arrow per pair: 12 arrows between distinct people plus 4 loops.

questions.topic: Reading a relation as a graph
questions.q: In the phone-number graph, (x, y) ∈ R means "x knows y's number". Ben knows Don's number but Don does not know Ben's. How is this drawn?
choices: An undirected edge between B and D
An arrow B → D and no arrow D → B
questions.explain: Each pair (x, y) is an arrow x → y. (B, D) ∈ R gives B → D; since (D, B) ∉ R there is no D → B. Order matters because the two facts are different.

questions.q: How is the pair (B, B) in a relation drawn in its directed graph?
choices: As a node with no arrows
As a loop from B to itself
questions.explain: A pair (x, x) is drawn as a **loop**: an arrow from the node back to itself. In the example it meant "Ben knows his own number".

questions.q: S = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 3)}. Which node(s) are adjacent to node 2 (i.e. y with (2, y) ∈ R)?
questions.explain: y is adjacent to x when (x, y) ∈ R, i.e. there is an arrow x → y. The only pair with first component 2 is (2, 1), so node 1 is adjacent to 2.

questions.q: A directed graph given as a set of ordered pairs and the same graph drawn as a diagram are equivalent: each can be reconstructed from the other.
questions.explain: Nodes are the elements of S and there is exactly one arrow per pair in R, so no information is lost either way. The course draws machines (state diagrams) this way.

questions.q: Why does this course review relations and directed graphs?
choices: To prove theorems about graph coloring
Because shortest-path algorithms are a main topic
Because machines in the course will be represented as directed graphs (state diagrams)
questions.explain: Machines (finite automata, later Turing machines) will be drawn as diagrams: nodes are states, arrows are transitions. Formally, labeled arrows are triples (p, symbol, q) — a ternary relation.

questions.q: In this course, 0 is a natural number.
questions.explain: The course (and its textbook) uses ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …} and writes ℕ⁺ = {1, 2, 3, …} for the positive naturals. Books differ; it is a convention. Note that Peano's original 1889 list started at 1.

questions.q: Why is ℤ = {…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …} not a proper *definition* of the integers?
choices: Because sets cannot contain negative numbers
Because "…" relies on the reader guessing the pattern; it is not a precise recipe a machine could follow
Because the elements are listed in order
questions.explain: The dots only work because the reader already knows the pattern; a computer (or a child) cannot follow them. An infinite set needs a finite, mechanical recipe — a recursive definition.

questions.q: Which are the undefined (primitive) terms in Peano's definition of the natural numbers?
questions.explain: Peano's system rests on three undefined terms: **natural (number), zero, successor**. Addition and multiplication are defined later from successor.

questions.q: Which is the recursive definition of ℕ used in the lesson?
choices: Basis: 0 ∈ ℕ. Step: if n ∈ ℕ then s(n) ∈ ℕ. Closure: n ∈ ℕ only if obtained from 0 by finitely many applications of s.
Basis: 0 ∈ ℕ. Step: if n ∈ ℕ then s(n) ∈ ℕ.
Basis: 0 ∈ ℕ. Step: if m, n ∈ ℕ then m + n ∈ ℕ. Closure: no one else.
ℕ is the set of all n such that n ∈ ℕ.
questions.explain: Basis 0; recursive step via the successor s; closure saying nothing else is natural. Option B omits closure; C uses addition, which is not yet defined; D is circular.

questions.q: In the Peano-style world, what is "2"?
questions.explain: There are no numerals yet — only 0 and successor. "2" is our abbreviation for s(s(0)), which is in ℕ by applying the recursive step twice starting from the basis.

questions.q: Which statement about Peano's 1889 work is accurate?
choices: It was written in English and started at 0
It was written in Latin and started at 1
It defined naturals using addition as a primitive
questions.explain: Peano published *Arithmetices principia* in Latin in 1889, and his original list started at **1**. Modern presentations (and this course) start at 0.

questions.q: Using m + 0 = m and m + s(n) = s(m + n), s(0) + s(s(0)) = s(s(…s(0)…)) with how many s's?
questions.explain: s(0) + s(s(0)) = s(s(0) + s(0)) = s(s(s(0) + 0)) = s(s(s(0))): three s's, i.e. 1 + 2 = 3. Each recursive step peels one s off the second argument until the basis m + 0 = m applies.

questions.q: What are the three parts of a recursive definition of a set, in order?
questions.explain: Basis (finitely many explicit elements), recursive step (operations building new elements from ones already in the set), closure ("no one else").

questions.q: What goes wrong if you leave out the closure clause?
choices: The recursive step can no longer be applied
The definition no longer excludes unwanted extra elements
questions.explain: Basis and step only say what **must** be in the set. Without closure, nothing rules out extra, unwanted elements, so the set is not pinned down. Always write it, even as "no one else".

questions.q: Why are recursive definitions needed mainly for infinite sets?
choices: A finite set can just be listed; an infinite set needs a finite recipe
Finite sets cannot be defined recursively at all
Infinite sets have no elements to list
Closure only works for infinite sets
questions.explain: A finite set can simply be listed. An infinite set cannot, so it needs a **finite** piece of text that mechanically generates exactly its elements — the idea behind grammars and automata later in the course.

questions.q: In "If t ∈ K, then t · a ∈ K", what is t?
choices: A fixed string equal to λ
A variable standing for any element already known to be in K
The last symbol of a string
A terminal symbol of the alphabet
questions.explain: t is a placeholder: any element already known to be in K. The rule says whichever t you pick from K, t · a is also in K.

questions.q: Which technique formally proves that a recursively defined set equals a target set (though it is not required in this course)?
choices: Proof by contradiction on the alphabet
questions.explain: **Structural induction** — induction over how elements are built from the basis by rule applications — shows soundness; completeness usually uses induction on string length. In class you instead generate elements (about 15) and eyeball them.

questions.q: If the first 15 elements generated by a recursive definition all belong to the target set, the definition is proved correct.
questions.explain: Generating elements is evidence, not proof. A wrong rule such as "if |t| ≥ 20 then t · a ∈ W" would look perfect on all short strings and only fail later. Only a proof rules that out.

questions.q: What is |λ|?
questions.explain: λ is the empty string: it contains no symbols, so its length is 0. (Many other books write ε.)

questions.q: What is ab · ba?
questions.explain: Concatenation writes the first string then the second: ab · ba = abba. Reversed, ba · ab = baab, so concatenation is not commutative.

questions.q: Which facts about concatenation hold for all strings u, v, w?
questions.explain: λ is an identity, lengths add, and concatenation is associative (so parentheses are omitted). It is not commutative: ab · ba ≠ ba · ab.

questions.q: Write a⁰ as a string (use the course's symbol for the empty string).
questions.explain: aⁿ is a concatenated with itself n times; zero copies is the empty string λ. E.g. a⁶ = aaaaaa.

questions.q: Why must the shortest strings of a target set (e.g. λ for even lengths, or a and b for odd lengths) appear in the basis?
choices: Because concatenation only makes strings longer, so they could never be generated
Because the basis must have exactly two elements
questions.explain: New elements come from concatenation, which never makes a string shorter. With nothing shorter to build from, the shortest elements can only enter through the basis.

questions.q: Which recursive definition generates exactly Σ* for Σ = {a, b} (all strings, including λ)?
choices: Basis λ ∈ K; step t · a, t · b ∈ K; closure
Basis a, b ∈ K; step t · a, t · b ∈ K; closure
Basis λ ∈ K; step t · a ∈ K; closure
Basis λ ∈ K; step t · aa, t · bb, t · ab, t · ba ∈ K; closure
questions.explain: Starting from λ and appending a or b in any order reaches every string. Option B misses λ; C only builds strings of a's; D only even lengths.

questions.q: For the set of even-length strings over {a, b}, what is the basis of the minimal definition?
questions.explain: |λ| = 0 is even, and λ can never be produced by concatenation, so it must be put in by the basis. Every other even string is built by appending two symbols.

questions.q: With basis λ, which recursive step generates exactly the even-length strings over {a, b}?
choices: t · aa, t · ab, t · ba, t · bb
questions.explain: Appending two symbols keeps an even length even, and the four pairs aa, ab, ba, bb cover every possible last two symbols. t · aa and t · bb alone miss e.g. ab; t · a, t · b would create odd strings.

questions.q: Adding the rule "if t ∈ W then t · aaaa ∈ W" to the minimal even-length definition makes the definition incorrect.
questions.explain: The rule adds 4 symbols, so it preserves evenness (it is sound); it just produces nothing new, since t · aaaa = (t · aa) · aa. Redundant rules are allowed: "better to have more than not enough".

questions.q: Definition X: Basis λ; step t · ab, t · ba, t · a; closure. Is X the set of even-length strings?
choices: No: t · a produces odd-length strings such as a
questions.explain: The rule t · a is **wrong**: from t = λ it gives a, which has odd length. (Also, t · ab and t · ba alone could never produce aa or bb.) A rule that produces even one string outside the target makes the definition incorrect.

questions.q: Which recursive definition gives exactly the odd-length strings over {a, b}?
choices: Basis a, b; step t · a, t · b; closure
Basis a, b; step t · aa, t · ab, t · ba, t · bb; closure
Basis λ; step t · aa, t · ab, t · ba, t · bb; closure
Basis a, b; no recursive step needed
questions.explain: Same recipe as even lengths (append two symbols) but a different basis: the two shortest odd strings, a and b. Appending one symbol (option A) would create aa; basis λ (C) is even.

questions.q: Odd-length definition with basis a, b, steps t · aa, t · ab, t · ba, t · bb, **plus** aa · t. The extra rule is:
choices: Necessary: without it aaa cannot be generated
questions.explain: If |t| is odd, |aa · t| = |t| + 2 is odd, so it never produces a wrong string; and the append rules already generate every odd string (aa · a = aaa = a · aa). So it is redundant — allowed.

questions.q: Applying the rules t · aa, t · ab, t · ba, t · bb to the four length-2 strings aa, ab, ba, bb gives how many distinct strings of length 4?
questions.explain: 4 choices of t × 4 rules = 16, all distinct — and that is every string of length 4, since 4 positions with 2 choices each gives 2⁴ = 16.

questions.q: When listing the elements of a set of strings to check a definition, how should you order them?
choices: In the order the rules were written
questions.explain: List shortest to longest (e.g. λ; aa, ab, ba, bb; then length 4) and stop once the pattern is visible. Alphabetical listing would run forever through aaaa… without ever reaching b.

questions.q: If a recursive definition generates the same string twice (e.g. aaaa from two different rules), the definition is flawed.
questions.explain: Repetition does not matter in a set, so generating a string again simply adds nothing new. It is not an error.

questions.q: Which definition gives exactly the strings over {a, b} that start with a?
choices: Basis λ; step a · t, t · b; closure
Basis a; step t · a; closure
Basis a; step t · a, t · b; closure
Basis a; step t · a, b · t; closure
questions.explain: The basis must be a (λ does not start with a), and appending at the **end** keeps the first symbol a. Prepending b (option D) would break that. First elements: a, aa, ab, aaa, aab, aba, abb.

questions.q: Which definition gives L = {a, aa, aaa, …}?
choices: Basis a ∈ L; step if t ∈ L then t · a ∈ L; closure
Basis λ ∈ L; step t · a ∈ L; closure
Basis a ∈ L; step t · aa ∈ L; closure
Basis a ∈ L; closure (no step needed)
questions.explain: The shortest element a goes in the basis, and appending a once more gives the next one. Basis λ would include the empty string, which is a⁰ with n = 0 < 1.
